content_text:
Hazardous waste volumes may grow 4M tons by 2033 due to manufacturing
A Veolia-backed report outlined the need to ensure capacity keeps up with the sector. The company said ongoing investments in semiconductors, autos and biotech are spurring new demand.
Published Sept. 23, 2026
Cole Rosengren 
Managing Editor 
Share 
Copy link 
Email 
LinkedIn 
X/Twitter 
Facebook 
Print 
License 
Add us on Google 
Ford F-150 trucks are assembled at a factory on Jan. 13, 2026, in Dearborn, Michigan. Increased manufacturing output is expected to lead to increased hazardous waste generation.
Anna Moneymaker via Getty Images
Listen to the article
6 min 
This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback .
Dive Brief:
U.S. hazardous waste generation could reach 37.4 million tons by 2033, up 5 million tons from 2023, according to a Veolia-commissioned report written by Charles River Associates. The report warns that a capacity shortfall of 1% could affect at least $27.5 billion in economic output over that time period.
Higher manufacturing activity is expected to account for 4 million of increased tonnage, driven by new investments in domestic production of semiconductors, pharmaceuticals, steel and more.
This comes as the overall hazardous waste sector’s revenues have nearly tripled from $3.6 billion in 2021 to almost $9 billion in 2023, according to the report.
Dive Insight:
The hazardous waste sector has seen heightened activity in recent years, including facility investments and notable M&A. Veolia North America, a division of the international environmental services giant, has been increasingly active with multiple acquisitions and an ongoing incinerator construction project in Arkansas.
The U.S. EPA currently estimates there is enough hazardous waste disposal capacity, but the report notes long timelines required to permit new facilities. It also cited the potential for surprise events such as the 2023 train derailment in East Palestine, Ohio; as well as extreme weather that can damage waste facilities or affect Superfund sites and in turn lead to new volumes.
Domestic manufacturing investments have also grown due to the reshoring of auto manufacturing, federal funding for emiconductor fabrication facilities and an uptick in biotech sites to create vaccines and weight-loss drugs, among other examples. This, in turn, comes with more hazardous and specialty waste streams.
Bob Cappadona, CEO of Veolia’s hazardous waste business in North America, said the company has secured several large clients in those sectors. This growth, coupled with logistical challenges experienced during the COVID-19 pandemic and Winter Storm Uri in 2021, spurred Veolia to take a fresh look at its approach to the U.S.
“The volume of material that was being managed within the hazardous waste network and the capacity to support it got out of sync,” during the pandemic, he said.
At the same time, some manufacturers are choosing to exit their own hazardous waste processing operations, which can be used to handle excess volumes that otherwise would be shipped offsite. 3M closed a Minnesota incinerator in 2021, and Alcoa sold an Arkansas site to Veolia in 2020.
“I think at times there was an assumption that there was going to be a wave that they were all going to shut down at the same time. We haven't seen that,” said Cappadona. “There's some other facilities that are going through similar evaluations.”
Veolia is now in the process of finalizing a 100,000-ton-per-year hazardous waste incinerator at that former Alcoa location, which it says will be the first H050-qualified thermal facility in the U.S. 
Manufacturing accounted for 90% of U.S. hazardous waste generation in 2023, followed by transportation. The report noted that its estimates of 2033 waste generation could be conservative if factors such as steel tariffs and artificial intelligence demand spur even greater investment.
Such investments present an opportunity for manufacturers to plan ahead for waste needs. Cappadona said some companies are approaching Veolia before they’ve even broken ground.
“The better decisions that are made at that point of generation have an impact on how that material may be able to be managed post-use of the original generator,” he said, citing one semiconductor client that’s been able to recycle 99% of its waste due in part to upfront sorting. In some cases, processes such as solvent recycling and wastewater treatment could also be handled on site.
In another example, Cappadona said Veolia is evaluating one opportunity to site its own operations in a neighboring facility to a semiconductor manufacturer to reduce transportation costs.
The EPA’s latest hazardous waste capacity assessment , released in 2025, estimated there’s enough permitted capacity to handle currently projected volumes through at least 2049. At the same time, it encouraged waste minimization efforts and suggested that states “to seek ways to develop new incineration and landfill capacity for the future.” 
An EPA spokesperson said this current hazardous waste assurance — required under the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation and Liability Act — expires Dec. 31, 2029. A new capacity assessment will be conducted at some point by then.
The Veolia-commissioned report notes there are currently 17 commercial hazardous waste landfills, 12 energy recovery facilities and 11 incinerators operating in the U.S. The number of hazardous waste landfills has declined, with sites owned by Arcwood Environmental, Clean Harbors, Republic Services and Veolia now managing the majority of tons. There have been more incinerator projects in recent years, led by Arcwood, Clean Harbors and Veolia.
To meet demand, Veolia is evaluating a potential expansion at its Port Arthur, Texas, incinerator, but there’s no set timeline. Cappadona said the company is currently taking steps to increase capacity through processing efficiencies at that site.
Acquisitions will continue to be part of the company’s capacity expansion plans. Cappadona cited two pending deals, one on the East Coast and one on the West, that are targeted to specific types of manufacturing needs. 
Cappadona also encouraged the waste sector to think beyond just landfill, incineration and fuel-blending capacity and pursue other technologies. 
He cited Veolia’s recent investment in an Arizona recycling facility for semiconductor material as well as the acquisition of a New England medical waste site for biotech material .
“Those are traditional treatment methods. What about the untraditional treatment methods?” he said, noting in some cases this could involve greenfield projects. “I think that's really the target for our group, how do we use those legacy older technologies in combination with some of the newer technologies to meet the demands of industry.”

BASF Conducts Feasibility Study for MDI Production Investment in India
Zacks Equity Research 
September 22, 2026 3 min read 
BAS.DE 
KRO 
BASFY 
RS 
AVNT 
BASF SE BASFY announced that it is evaluating a potential investment in India to establish a methylene diphenyl diisocyanate (MDI) production complex in Dahej, Gujarat, to address the growing regional customer demand. The company is in the advanced stages of a feasibility study and has secured an industrial land parcel through its Indian subsidiary, BASF India Polyurethanes Private Limited. 
MDI is a key raw material used in polyurethane products for building insulation, refrigeration, automotive components, furniture and consumer goods. The investment plan is aligned with BASF's 'Winning Ways' strategy and local-for-local approach, which focuses on strengthening core businesses and expanding its manufacturing footprint. 
The potential facility would ensure reliable supply of locally produced MDI to customers across India and neighboring markets. The investment decision will depend on the feasibility study's outcome and remain subject to necessary approvals. 
The proposed project would complement BASF's global MDI production network, which includes facilities in the United States, Belgium, China and South Korea. Meanwhile, the company's $1 billion MDI expansion project in Geismar, LA, is entering its final phase. 
BASF's existing operations in Dahej, including an MDI splitter and polyurethane production facilities, provide a strong foundation for the potential investment. India's expanding urbanization, infrastructure development and manufacturing activity are expected to support demand for high-performance materials, creating growth opportunities for BASF India. 
BASFY's shares have gained 17.2% in the past year compared with the industry's 1.7% decline in the same period.

Fiona Craig 
September 22, 2026 2 min read

Semiconductor ©PickPik Valens Semiconductor (NYSE:VLN) has entered into a collaboration agreement with onsemi (NASDAQ:ON) to develop a cost-optimised image sensor incorporating MIPI A-PHY connectivity for high-volume automotive camera applications. 
The agreement, announced on 22 September 2026, focuses on integrating Valens' connectivity technology directly into onsemi's image sensors, targeting the 3-megapixel (3MP) segment. 
The companies aim to provide automotive manufacturers and Tier 1 suppliers with an integrated solution that supports adoption of the MIPI A-PHY standard. 
Collaboration Targets Simplified Automotive Camera Design 
Under the agreement, Valens will work with onsemi to incorporate MIPI A-PHY connectivity into the image sensor itself. 
The integrated approach is intended to reduce the number of separate components required in automotive camera systems while supporting industry-standard connectivity. 
Ahmed Salem, Vice President and General Manager of the Intelligent Sensing Group at onsemi, said the collaboration aims to enable: 
"a more streamlined camera architecture that reduces component count, supports industry standards, and ultimately makes advanced vision systems easier to deploy." 
The companies are targeting applications where manufacturers require cost-efficient camera systems that can be produced in high volumes. 
Companies Focus on 3MP Automotive Camera Market 
Most automotive image sensors currently target resolutions between 1 and 3 megapixels, according to the companies. 
Valens and onsemi said their planned 3MP offering addresses this established market while also targeting demand from automotive manufacturers upgrading to higher-resolution camera systems. 
The collaboration is intended to provide an additional route for original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) and Tier 1 suppliers to incorporate MIPI A-PHY connectivity into their camera designs. 
MIPI A-PHY is an industry standard designed for high-speed sensor connectivity in automotive applications. 
Partnership Expands Valens' A-PHY Product Offering 
Valens has previously announced design wins with multiple automotive OEMs for its VA7000 MIPI A-PHY chipsets. 
The collaboration with onsemi extends its approach to include connectivity integrated directly into image sensors, complementing its existing standalone chipset products. 
Yoram Salinger, Chief Executive of Valens Semiconductor, said the new offering: 
"complements Valens' existing solutions, bringing A-PHY to a much broader range of use cases." 
He added that working with onsemi strengthens the technology ecosystem by giving: 
Story Continues 
"automakers the supplier choice they expect from an industry standard." 
The agreement establishes a development partnership between the two semiconductor companies. Neither a commercial launch date nor financial terms were disclosed in the announcement.

content_text:
Charles River’s (CRL) Vaccine Push Meets A Bumpy Quarter
Maham Fatima 
September 21, 2026 4 min read 
CRL 
-1.51% 
6547.TWO 
+0.79% 
On August 20, Charles River Laboratories (NYSE: CRL ) announced a collaboration with Medigen Vaccine Biologics Corp/MVC to apply next-generation sequencing to MVC's new multivalent enterovirus vaccine program. On its own, the deal is small. But it shows Charles River finding fresh uses for the sequencing technology it picked up through an earlier acquisition, and it lands just two weeks after a mixed second quarter that raised guidance but posted a GAAP loss. Investors are left weighing two different stories at once. 
Charles River's (CRL) Vaccine Push Meets A Bumpy Quarter Sequencing Its Way Into Vaccines 
Under the collaboration, Charles River will characterize and validate the virus seed bank behind MVC's next-generation enterovirus vaccine, using Next-Generation Sequencing to support the chemistry, manufacturing, and controls work needed to satisfy global regulators. MVC already has a commercialized enterovirus vaccine approved in Taiwan and Vietnam, so this is a company with a track record picking Charles River as its partner for the harder next step. 
The two companies say they will also explore other vaccine programs together, which points to more than a one-off contract. That NGS work traces back to Charles River's acquisition of Pathoquest, a specialist in sequencing-based testing for biopharmaceuticals, and the same capability turned up again in the second quarter, when Charles River struck a testing collaboration with Arovella Therapeutics on cancer treatments and joined Eli Lilly's TuneLab platform to support drug discovery. 
Layered on an AI-enabled digital pathology tool meant to speed up study turnaround, the DSA segment posted its highest net book-to-bill in nearly four years, prompting management to raise both organic revenue and non-GAAP earnings guidance for 2026. The Manufacturing segment's non-GAAP operating margin climbed to 37.8% from 32.8% a year earlier, and Charles River kept buying back stock, spending $300 million on 1.7 million shares through the first half of the year, with $700 million left on its authorization. 
A Quarter Of Mixed Signals 
The second quarter's headline numbers were not as clean. Revenue fell 2.7% year over year to $1.00 billion, and organic growth of just 0.1% was still the best the company has managed since 2023, a sign of how sluggish the prior stretch had been. The Research Models and Services segment kept sliding, with revenue down 1.8% as demand for small research models weakened in North America even as China picked up some slack. Charles River posted a GAAP loss of $0.03 per share, versus a profit of $1.06 a year ago, almost entirely because of a $63.7 million loss tied to divesting its CDMO and Cell Solutions businesses along with certain European Discovery Services sites. 
Story Continues 
Even stripping out those one-time items, non-GAAP earnings per share fell 3.2% to $3.02, as higher study-related costs in DSA and rising corporate expenses pushed the non-GAAP operating margin down to 20.5% from 22.1%. Management is raising its non-GAAP guidance for the year. Still, it cut GAAP earnings per share guidance to reflect the divestiture losses, a reminder that the portfolio cleanup carries real accounting costs even as it clears the way for the businesses Charles River wants to grow. 
What The Numbers Whisper 
The number of hedge funds holding Charles River rose to 47 from 43 the prior quarter, a modest pickup in institutional interest. Short sellers have not backed off, with 6.14% of the float sold short, enough to reflect a real bear camp rather than passing skepticism. The stock trades at a forward P/E of 22.47 as of September 21, a multiple that assumes earnings growth resumes rather than one that prices in more quarters like the one just reported. Rising fund ownership alongside meaningful short interest suggests the market is still arguing with itself over which of Charles River's two stories will win out. 
Two Stories, One Stock 
Charles River is trying to prove it can extend its testing expertise into new corners of drug and vaccine development while trimming the businesses that no longer fit. The vaccine collaboration and the guidance raise say that strategy is gaining traction. The GAAP loss and the shrinking core segments say the transition still has real costs to absorb. For the growth story to hold, the DSA rebound and the new sequencing partnerships need to keep compounding into next year. For the skeptics to be right, the divestitures need to keep generating charges large enough to offset whatever operational progress shows up underneath.

Applied Materials Commits $5 Billion to India as Chip Manufacturing Expands
Vardah Gill 
September 21, 2026 3 min read 
AMAT 
-8.16% 
Applied Materials, Inc. (NASDAQ: AMAT ) plans to invest $5 billion in India over the next decade, expanding its research, supply-chain, and workforce capabilities as India tries to establish itself as a major semiconductor manufacturing hub. 
The announcement came at SEMICON India, where more than 600 companies from 52 countries participated. India has committed more than $21 billion in semiconductor incentives and expects domestic semiconductor consumption to reach $110 billion by 2030. Applied's investment is therefore aimed at building a longer-term presence in an emerging semiconductor ecosystem rather than generating an immediate revenue contribution. 
Applied Materials (AMAT) - Among Billionaire Steven Cohen’s Top 11 Dividend Stock Picks India Investment Could Expand Applied Materials' Long-Term Growth 
The investment could give Applied Materials, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMAT) an early position in a market that is attempting to diversify semiconductor production beyond established hubs such as China and Taiwan. India has already approved 12 semiconductor projects under its incentive program, while commercial production has begun at some chip-packaging facilities. As more fabs and packaging facilities become operational, Applied could capture demand for deposition, etch, inspection, packaging, and other process equipment. Its existing portfolio spans these manufacturing stages, giving the company multiple opportunities to participate as India's ecosystem develops. 
The investment also fits Applied's current growth cycle. In fiscal Q3 2026, revenue reached a record $9.12 billion, up 25% year over year, while gross margin rose to 50.3% and operating income increased to $3.08 billion. Applied generated a record $3.04 billion in operating cash flow during the quarter. The company has said strong AI-driven demand is supporting leading-edge logic, DRAM and advanced packaging, while it expects semiconductor-equipment growth to remain strong through 2027. A larger Indian R&D and supply-chain footprint could therefore support capacity and customer diversification as semiconductor investment expands globally. 
Applied Materials Faces Execution Risks With Its India Expansion 
The biggest risk is that India's semiconductor ambitions may take considerably longer to translate into equipment revenue. Reuters reported that India still has no large-scale chip fabrication facility in commercial production, while Tata Electronics' planned $10 billion fab in Gujarat has been delayed by nearly two years. That means Applied Materials, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMAT) could commit substantial capital well before the local customer base generates meaningful equipment demand. The $5 billion commitment spread over ten years also represents a long-duration capital allocation rather than an immediate earnings catalyst. 
Story Continues 
The investment could also pressure returns if India's manufacturing buildout progresses more slowly than expected. Applied already faces significant geopolitical exposure: its SEC filing says export restrictions have limited its China market and increased exposure to Chinese competitors. The company also paid $253 million in 2026 to settle a U.S. Commerce Department inquiry involving certain China shipments. At the same time, investors have questioned whether Applied can maintain its recent growth and margins; Reuters noted that its fourth-quarter revenue forecast of $10.25 billion came with a roughly 50.4% margin outlook amid increasing competition. Expanding in India could diversify geopolitical exposure, but it does not eliminate execution, regulatory, or capital-allocation risks. 
Conclusion 
Applied Materials, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMAT)'s $5 billion India commitment strengthens its long-term positioning in a market targeting $110 billion of semiconductor consumption by 2030, while aligning with the company's need to expand capacity as AI drives demand for advanced chips and packaging. The main limitation is timing: India's fab ecosystem remains immature, with major projects still facing delays. Consequently, the investment is more directly relevant to Applied's long-term geographic diversification and competitive positioning than to near-term revenue or earnings.

Tata Electronics, Sumitomo Chemical sign MoU to strengthen semiconductor supply chain
By Nitisha Dubey 
Share
Facebook

September 21, 2026 
Tata Electronics is building India’s first commercial 12-inch (300 mm) semiconductor Fab in Dholera 
Tata Electronics has signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Japan-based Sumitomo Chemical to strengthen India’s semiconductor materials supply chain and support the development of a domestic semiconductor manufacturing ecosystem.
Under the agreement, the companies will explore a collaboration under which Sumitomo Chemical will supply semiconductor materials to Tata Electronics’ upcoming semiconductor Fab in Dholera, Gujarat. The materials will include photoresists, functional chemicals and high-purity chemicals such as hydrogen peroxide, isopropyl alcohol, ammonia water and sulfuric acid.
The two companies will also explore the manufacturing of semiconductor materials and high-purity chemicals in India, with Tata Electronics supporting Sumitomo Chemical in evaluating opportunities for local production.
Dr. Randhir Thakur, CEO and MD, Tata Electronics, said the partnership would help strengthen the supply of high-quality materials for the company’s upcoming Fab while contributing to India-Japan cooperation in the semiconductor sector.
- Advertisement - 
Satoshi Honda, Managing Executive Officer, Sumitomo Chemical, said the company aims to contribute to a stable supply of semiconductor materials and a more diversified semiconductor supply chain in India by leveraging its expertise in photoresists, functional chemicals and high-purity chemicals.
Tata Electronics is building India’s first commercial 12-inch (300 mm) semiconductor Fab in Dholera, Gujarat, with a planned investment of $11 billion. The facility is expected to manufacture chips for applications including automotive, mobile devices and artificial intelligence.
The company has also partnered with Taiwan’s PSMC to gain access to semiconductor technologies spanning 28nm to 110nm nodes. The partnership with Sumitomo Chemical is expected to further strengthen the Fab’s supply ecosystem by adding capabilities across semiconductor materials and high-purity chemicals.
The collaboration comes as India works to build a more diversified and resilient semiconductor manufacturing ecosystem, with domestic capabilities in materials, equipment, manufacturing, process technologies and chip design.

title: Onsemi to Eliminate Power Module Assembly by Integrating Chips Into Wafers - THE ELEC, Korea Electronics Industry Media
source: Google News: THE ELEC, Korea Electronics Industry Media
publisher: THE ELEC, Korea Electronics Industry Media
query: "onsemi" (Korea OR Korean) after:2026-09-01 before:2026-10-01
content_text:
Onsemi has unveiled a new technology that uses silicon wafers as substrates for power semiconductor packages, integrating power semiconductors and control chips into a single structure to make power systems smaller and more efficient.
​Onsemi on Sept. 18 unveiled its Embedded Power Platform (EPP).
​EPP is similar in concept to embedded-die technology, which places power semiconductor chips inside a package substrate. The difference is that EPP uses a 12-inch silicon wafer as the package substrate instead of a conventional printed circuit board (PCB).
​Conventional power modules mount multiple power semiconductor chips on a substrate and connect them with metal wires. EPP integrates multiple chips, including silicon (Si), silicon carbide (SiC) and gallium nitride (GaN) power semiconductors, as well as drivers and controllers, directly onto a wafer.
​Onsemi said the architecture can increase power density by three to five times compared with existing solutions. Shorter connections between chips reduce power losses caused by current flow and voltage fluctuations generated during switching. The company also said the use of silicon, which has high thermal conductivity, improves heat dissipation.
​Key applications include traction inverters for electric vehicles and artificial intelligence (AI) data centers.
​A traction inverter converts direct-current electricity from a battery into alternating-current electricity used to drive a motor. Onsemi said EPP can increase inverter power density by up to four times and reduce power losses by 15%.
​Another feature is that a single basic architecture can be used across different power ratings. Automakers would not need to develop separate inverters for entry-level and high-performance vehicles. Onsemi said this could shorten development time by up to four months.
​Onsemi said Japanese automaker Subaru is participating as an early partner for EPP. Subaru will receive engineering samples and simulation models from Onsemi and evaluate whether EPP can be applied to future electrified vehicles.
​The company said applying EPP to solid-state circuit breakers for AI data centers could reduce product size by 50% and lower operating temperatures by 20%.
​"Semiconductors and packages have been treated as separate technologies for decades," said Hassane El-Khoury, president and CEO of Onsemi. "EPP integrates silicon itself as part of the system architecture."
​Onsemi plans to begin supplying EPP samples to key customers in the automotive and AI sectors this year.

Amkor Technology eyes expanded investment in South Jeolla-Gwangju region
by 서 인주 
Published : Sept. 20, 2026 - 08:58:48
View Korean Original
Link copied!
Amkor Technology announced in June a plan to add six factory buildings on idle land within its Gwangju factory in the Cheomdan district of Buk-gu and to expand the site in phases through 2035. 
Whether Amkor Technology, a global semiconductor packaging company, will expand its investment in the South Jeolla-Gwangju region is drawing close attention. Having announced a 1 trillion won investment plan for Gwangju, the company is reportedly reviewing a further expansion into the Cheomdan 3 district, with an eye toward creating synergies with the 800 trillion won Honam semiconductor industry cluster and linking up with the AI sector.
With the launch of the South Jeolla-Gwangju integrated special city, which brings added administrative licensing support and broader investment infrastructure, observers are watching whether the investment will grow beyond its original scale.
Amkor Technology has also resolved a wastewater treatment problem that had long been a source of concern.
The South Jeolla-Gwangju integrated special city and Jangseong-gun signed a semiconductor wastewater treatment MOU at the Muan government complex on Friday to support Amkor Technology Korea's semiconductor factory investment.
The two sides agreed to work together to resolve the wastewater treatment issue, which had been identified as a major obstacle to expanding Amkor's semiconductor factory. The development stands in contrast to 2022, when Amkor shelved its Gwangju investment plan and instead expanded its production lines in Vietnam.
Amkor announced in June a plan to add six factory buildings on idle land within its Gwangju factory in the Cheomdan district of Buk-gu and to expand the site in phases through 2035.
The city had drawn up a plan to link Amkor's expanded wastewater output to the Gwangju No. 1 Sewage Treatment Plant, but the facility had in effect reached its capacity limit, creating an additional wastewater treatment problem.
The city then proposed connecting the wastewater to Jangseong-gun's public wastewater treatment facility. After Jangseong-gun accepted the proposal, the two sides concluded the agreement.
The two local governments plan to build the infrastructure needed to handle wastewater generated during semiconductor manufacturing in time for Amkor's large-scale investment, and to establish an administrative support framework.
They agreed to build wastewater treatment facilities on a schedule that will not disrupt factory operation timelines, and to cooperate at every stage — from licensing and facility construction to future operation and management.
South Jeolla-Gwangju Special City Mayor Min Hyeong-bae said the city would "focus its efforts on expanding essential infrastructure and providing administrative support so that Amkor's investment proceeds without a hitch."

content_text:
News 
Fortaegis Technologies Raises $50 Million Series A to Deploy Hardware-Rooted Quantum-Safe Secure Compute Architecture
September 19, 2026 · 1 min read
Share 
Copy link 
Amsterdam-based hardware security startup Fortaegis Technologies has closed an oversubscribed $50 million Series A funding round to accelerate commercial production and global deployment of its full-stack Secure Compute architecture. Led by returning investor Serendipity Capital , the syndicate includes strategic semiconductor, industrial, and defense backers TEL Venture Capital (the CVC arm of Tokyo Electron ), ASML , TNO , Prodrive Technologies , NP-Hard Ventures , NovaCapital , Access Ventures , and Coalition Capital .
The company’s executive leadership and board include Ilyas Khan (Founder of Quantinuum ) as Chairman, Boudewijn Wijnands as Founder and CEO, and Chris Miller (author of Chip War ) as a U.S. Board Member. Fortaegis’s technology addresses hardware security threats posed by high-throughput AI workloads and post-quantum decryption risks. The Fortaegis Silicon Platform provides a full-stack architecture spanning hardware, firmware, cryptography, and software that roots security directly in physical silicon properties.
[ Fortaegis Series A Financing & Architecture Overview ] 
Financing & Leadership Hardware & Cryptographic Architecture Deployment & Product Roadmap 
• $50 Million Series A 
• Lead: Serendipity Capital
• Strategic: ASML, TEL VC, TNO, Prodrive
• Chairman: Ilyas Khan (Quantinuum) • Physical silicon-rooted trust & identity
• Dynamic, quantum-safe key generation
• Machine-to-machine connections >200× faster
• Zero permanent on-chip key storage • Form Factors: Server rack, edge, embedded
• Commercial FPGA scaling across US, EU, SG, JP
• Dedicated custom ASIC roadmap development
• Targets: AI data centers, defense, telecom 
By extracting cryptographic entropy from microscopic physical manufacturing variations in silicon, the architecture generates dynamic, quantum-resistant encryption keys on demand without storing keys permanently on-chip, eliminating key-theft attack vectors. Fortaegis reports holding 17 patents (with 14 pending) and achieving secure machine-to-machine connection speeds over 200 times faster than conventional software cryptographic approaches in customer evaluations. Capital from the round will scale FPGA deployment and advance its custom ASIC development pipeline across data center, defense, telecommunications, and autonomous infrastructure markets.

title: Mitsubishi Chemical deepens AI infrastructure bet with NLM Photonics investment - Indiatimes
query: ("Mitsubishi Chemical" OR "Mitsubishi Chemical Group") ("press release" OR "investor relations" OR earnings OR announcement OR investment OR expansion OR acquisition OR partnership OR Korea) after:2026-09-01 before:2026-10-01
content_text:
Mitsubishi Chemical deepens AI infrastructure bet with NLM Photonics investment 
Mitsubishi Chemical has invested in NLM Photonics through Diamond Edge Ventures as AI data-centre traffic strains optical networks. The Washington State startup is developing organic electro-optic materials aimed at faster, lower-power optical modulation, with the deal highlighting growing strategic interest in photonics and advanced materials. 
ETChemicals 
Published On Sep 18, 2026 at 12:15 PM IST
Share Icon Copy Link Share on Whatsapp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook 
Bookmark 
Generative AI is forcing data-centre operators to rethink one of the most overlooked parts of the digital stack: how data moves between chips, servers and racks. Against that backdrop, Mitsubishi Chemical Corporation has chosen to back a US startup building the materials that could help ease that pressure, according to Indian Chemical News . 
The investment, routed through Diamond Edge Ventures, Inc. , Mitsubishi Chemical 's corporate venture capital arm, forms part of NLM Photonics ' Series A2 round led by Pangaea Ventures . The deal signals how materials groups are moving closer to the AI infrastructure race, where performance gains increasingly depend on advances in photonics rather than only on semiconductors and cloud hardware. 
Why optical interconnects matter in the AI build-out 
The latest wave of AI deployment has sharply increased the amount of data that must be shifted inside data centres. That has lifted the importance of optical interconnects, the communication links that enable high-speed data transmission while helping manage energy use. As workloads grow heavier, these links are becoming a strategic bottleneck for operators trying to keep speed, latency and power consumption in balance. 
Mitsubishi Chemical said materials used in optical modulation are emerging as a critical area for differentiated device performance. In practical terms, that means the chemistry inside photonic devices is becoming as important as the hardware architecture itself, especially when the industry is trying to push more data through the same physical footprint without a matching rise in electricity demand. 
What NLM Photonics is building 
NLM Photonics is based in Washington State and develops organic electro-optic materials for next-generation optical communications. The startup was founded on more than two decades of research at the University of Washington , giving it a scientific base that has been shaped by academic work rather than by a conventional hardware manufacturing playbook. 
Its Selerion materials are designed for use with silicon photonic devices to form hybrid silicon-organic photonic integrated circuits, or PICs. These are intended to support optical modulation at higher speeds and with lower power consumption than older inorganic approaches. The pitch is straightforward: if the materials can be integrated reliably into semiconductor-style production, they could help make AI data movement faster and more efficient. 
Manufacturing realism is now part of the pitch 
The investment case is not being built only on laboratory promise. Curtis Schickner , president of Diamond Edge Ventures , said the attraction lies in the combination of scientific depth and manufacturability. He argued that optical interconnects have become one of the real constraints in AI infrastructure, and that the remaining gains are concentrated in the materials used in modulators. Schickner added that NLM has shown organic electro-optic materials can be processed in ways that fit how the semiconductor industry actually builds devices. 
That framing matters because many advanced materials programmes stall when they move from research to production. For venture investors and strategic backers alike, the question is no longer whether a material works in a lab setting, but whether it can be handled at scale, incorporated into existing supply chains and delivered with consistent yields. Mitsubishi Chemical's backing suggests it sees NLM as one of the rarer cases that may clear that hurdle. 
A strategic fit with Mitsubishi Chemical's broader agenda 
The investment also aligns with Mitsubishi Chemical's management vision, KAITEKI Vision 35, under which advanced data processing and telecommunications are among the identified business focus areas. The group said it wants to deepen its understanding of next-generation optical communications, including optoelectronic integration, while also pursuing new business opportunities through its materials technologies. 
That approach reflects a wider trend among large industrial groups: rather than waiting for the AI boom to flow only to chipmakers and cloud providers, they are looking for entry points in the enabling layers that make those systems faster, cooler and more power efficient. Materials science, once seen as a long-cycle support function, is increasingly being treated as a strategic lever in digital infrastructure. 
What the deal says about the next phase of AI infrastructure 
The transaction comes at a time when the economics of AI are being shaped as much by power and connectivity as by model quality. Data centres need more than compute capacity. They also need interconnects that can move data at scale without causing energy costs to spiral. That is why optical technologies are drawing more attention from strategic investors, especially those with deep materials or manufacturing expertise. 
For NLM Photonics, the round provides validation from a major industrial backer as it works to commercialise a niche with broad implications. For Mitsubishi Chemical, the move is a way to position itself closer to the next generation of telecom and computing infrastructure, where the winners may be the groups that can help solve the bottlenecks others overlook. 
As AI workloads continue to expand, the pressure on data-centre networks is unlikely to ease soon. Investments such as this point to a broader shift in which the race for AI advantage is no longer confined to software and chips. It is also moving into the chemistry of light, the design of modulators and the materials that make faster, lower-power communications possible.

content_text:
Merck KGaA expands life science manufacturing hub in Bengaluru 
The move is the latest in a growing list of investments geared at bolstering India’s global footprint.
Josh Abbott , News Editor, BioProcess International September 18, 2026
schedule 2 Min Read 
stock.adobe.com 
link 
German life science and pharmaceutical company Merck KGaA has announced an expansion of its manufacturing facility in Bengaluru, India, to strengthen its production and supply operations in the Asia-Pacific region. 
Dhananjay Singh, managing director of Merck India’s Life Science business, said the company will invest €13 million (about US$15 million) in its Jigani, Bengaluru site to expand its biology and chemistry capabilities. 
According to a press release, the Jigani site will manufacture biological buffers and raw materials for diagnostic applications used in DNA research, cell culture, diagnostics, and drug manufacturing. 
The expansion will add about 2,900 square meters of new capabilities to Merck’s 40,460 square-meter campus. The site already has established capabilities in specialty and fine chemicals, custom synthesis, and catalog product manufacturing. 
“This investment will reinforce our global supply chain and support the ‘Make in India’ initiative,” Singh said. “We appreciate the continued collaboration from DPIIT, the Heavy Water Board, the Government of Karnataka, and Invest India as Merck expands Jigani.” 
Related: 53Biologics talks industry in Spain as company unveils $2.25m infrastructure expansion 
The country launched its Make in India initiative in 2014 to support its growth as a global design and manufacturing hub. 
“Merck’s Bengaluru manufacturing hub shows what the India–Germany partnership can achieve when world-class German enterprise meets India's manufacturing ambition,” added Shri Amardeep Singh Bhatia, IAS, secretary to the government of India, Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT), Ministry of Commerce and Industry. “In the year we celebrate 75 years of diplomatic relations, Merck will make advanced materials in Bengaluru for pharmaceutical research and semiconductor manufacturing, for India and for the world, in the true spirit of Make in India.” 
Big moves in India 
“India is emerging as an increasingly important hub for life science innovation and manufacturing,” said Singh during his remarks about the Merck expansion. 
Indeed, the South Asian country is becoming one of the most exciting global biotech hubs to follow. In addition to attracting international investment from industry giants such as Merck, India is headquarters to a growing ecosystem of homegrown companies that are making big moves. Earlier this week, contract development and manufacturing organization (CDMO) Shilpa Biologicals announced a biosimilar licensing agreement with Saudi Arabia-based SPIMACO Bio. And as part of an effort to accelerate peptide manufacturing, Hyderabad-based Neuland Laboratories recently announced that its first commercial peptide manufacturing module is now operational, with further expansion in its capacity underway. 
Related: Altruist Biologics preps for production following EMA GMP certification

Besi’s advanced packaging portfolio will help accelerate technology readiness at Tata Electronics’ semiconductor packaging facility in Jagiroad, Assam

Tata Electronics, a pioneering leader in India’s electronics and semiconductor manufacturing sector, and Besi, a leading Dutch provider of semiconductor assembly solutions, have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to strengthen advanced packaging capabilities in India.
Advertisment 
Add DQIndia Info As A Trusted Source
Tata Electronics is investing $3 billion for India’s first indigenous semiconductor packaging facility in Jagiroad, Assam. As part of the collaboration, Tata Electronics will leverage Besi’s extensive portfolio of advanced packaging equipment and technologies.  
The partnership aligns closely with the next phase of India’s semiconductor program, which seeks to establish a self-sufficient and globally competitive domestic OSAT industry. The partnership also reflects the growing momentum in India-Netherlands semiconductor cooperation following the MoU on partnership on semiconductors and related emerging technologies signed by the two countries. 
The partnership will assess opportunities to strengthen the local semiconductor equipment support ecosystem, facilitate technical collaboration, and enhance long-term equipment readiness for Tata Electronics' semiconductor packaging operations. Leveraging Besi’s extensive portfolio of advanced packaging solutions and global expertise, the collaboration will support the technology readiness of Tata Electronics’ semiconductor packaging facility in Jagiroad, Assam, while advancing its journey toward next-generation packaging capabilities.  
Advertisment 
Through this partnership, Besi will also evaluate initiatives to support engineering capability development, knowledge-sharing programs and specialized training and certification of Tata Electronics employees, to improve operational flexibility and efficiency. Both companies will work together to develop a shared technology roadmap and innovative processes to enable mutual, long-term growth and build a resilient and globally competitive supply chain in India. 
Dr. Randhir Thakur, CEO & MD, Tata Electronics, said: “Advanced packaging is rapidly becoming one of the most critical differentiators in semiconductor innovation. We are delighted to partner with Besi, a global leader in advanced packaging equipment. By combining Besi's world-class expertise with Tata Electronics' growing manufacturing platform, we aim to accelerate the development of advanced packaging capabilities in India, foster innovation, and help establish a robust semiconductor ecosystem that serves both domestic and global customers.” 
Richard Blickman, CEO and Chairman, Besi, said: “For over three decades, Besi has strived to create long-term value for stakeholders. Through this collaboration, our diverse range of advanced packaging solutions will support Tata Electronics' vision of becoming a global leader in semiconductor manufacturing. The partnership also reflects our shared commitment to innovation, technology development and the advancement of the semiconductor industry.”

India India Secures Up to $12 Billion in Semiconductor Investment Pledges Under Semicon 2.0 
September 17, 2026 651 1 minute read 
Facebook X LinkedIn Tumblr Pinterest Reddit VKontakte Odnoklassniki Pocket 
New Delhi — India has secured semiconductor investment commitments worth between $11 billion and $12 billion under Semicon 2.0, the second phase of the government’s semiconductor program, Union Electronics and IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said Thursday.
Speaking at Semicon India 2026, Vaishnaw said the commitments cover semiconductor equipment, materials, gases, chemicals and substrates, with the investments expected to materialize over the next two to three years.
The minister said companies will decide where to locate their semiconductor projects based on factors including policy certainty, government support and the strength of the surrounding ecosystem.
“Industry chooses the location depending upon where they feel more comfortable, how much policy certainty they see, what kind of support they see from governments, from the other ecosystem fields,” he said.
Semicon 2.0, approved with an outlay of Rs 1.27 lakh crore, focuses on chip design, semiconductor equipment and materials, fabrication plants, advanced packaging, research and development, and workforce development.
At the event, Tata Electronics signed an agreement with Ascendas First Space to develop a 363-acre vendor park that will support the supplier ecosystem surrounding its semiconductor fabrication plant in Dholera, Gujarat.
Tata Electronics also signed agreements with Fujifilm to localize critical semiconductor materials and with JSR Corporation for photoresists and advanced chemicals for the Dholera plant.
The program could attract about Rs 4 lakh crore in investment and support roughly Rs 2 lakh crore in semiconductor production over its duration, according to a recent report.
Fiscal incentives include 40% capital expenditure support for silicon fabrication plants on a pari-passu basis and up to 75% combined central and state government support for research, development and talent initiatives. (Source: IANS)

Robigo Bio eyes commercialization for its ag biologicals with Leaps by Bayer investment
September 17, 2026 | Jennifer Marston 
Agtech 
Biomanufacturing & biologicals 
Investing 
Startups & funding 
US & Canada 
Dr. Andee Wallace, Founder and CEO of Robigo. 
Image credit: Robigo Bio 
Robigo Bio has closed a Series A financing round to accelerate the commercial launch of its crop biological products, which the company claims can match or outperform synthetic chemistries instead of merely complementing them.
Importantly, these products will be simple for growers to integrate into their existing operations, says Dr. Andee Wallace, founder and CEO of Robigo.
“Growers shouldn’t have to choose between a product that works and one that’s affordable or sustainable. If you go out and talk with growers, you know what they want: something that’s simple that works with what they’re doing today.”
This, she adds, is exactly what Robigo aims to do with its engineered microbes.
Leaps by Bayer led the round, with participation from Illumina Ventures , SVG Thrive , Congruent Ventures , and Endeavor8 . Financial terms were not disclosed.
Cambridge, Massachusetts-based Robigo has two products currently gearing up for commercial launch. One, an engineered microbial seed treatment for soybean Sudden Death Syndrome, is slated for launch in 2028. A second, which targets fusarium wilt in lettuce and berries, will launch in 2029.
Funding will also support the company’s expansion into work on soil-borne pathogens in broad-acre crops, which Robigo claims is a $10 billion market.
Close up of soybean sudden death syndrome. Image credit: Robigo 
Engineering vs wild-type microbes 
Nearly all commercial microbial products on the market today use wild-type organisms—naturally occurring microbes selected for a useful characteristic, such as antifungal properties or nitrogen-fixing bacterium. Product development is more about finding the right strain of such microbes rather than engineering something.
Robigo takes a different approach. Instead of finding a microbe with fungal-fighting properties, it chooses one then “programs” it to produce the desired active ingredients. Robigo starts with microbes chosen for their shelf stability and manufacturing economics, then engineers in new traits computationally, including both the active bioingredients and safety parameters, claims Wallace.
“We identify microbes that serve as a really solid foundation to build high-performing products on top of — they have the shelf stability, they have the manufacturing capabilities to be cost-effective — and then we engineer in these new traits that allow us to be much higher performing than what biologicals are doing today, and also have a really improved safety profile,” she adds.
It is, she claims, “an entirely different way to develop microbial and biological products from what’s been historically done.”
These engineered microbes are applied as a one-time seed treatment and continuously produce and deliver active ingredients throughout the season, with no change to existing grower workflows. Critically, Robigo says they don’t require cold-chain storage, which has been a longstanding logistical headache for ag biological products.
The company’s proprietary ARGO platform ties these capabilities together across three components: microbial strain engineering, strain selection, and computational design of the bioactive compounds the microbes produce. Together, Robigo claims the platform can take a new biological product from design to field-tested in under 20 months. The industry norm is roughly three to five years.
Robigo’s first field trials last year marked what it believes is a regulatory first: field deployment of a living engineered microbe expressing new traits, cleared through the USDA and the EPA.
Early data from those trials has been encouraging, says Wallace. The soybean SDS treatment is on track to match the performance of commercially available chemistries at half the cost. That’s no small feat at a time when SDS causes an estimated $200–$500 million in annual losses for U.S. soybean farmers.
The fusarium wilt product for specialty crops showed a 3x yield increase compared to untreated controls.
Dr. Andee Wallace in the lab. Image credit: Robigo Bio 
Building a biologicals engine 
The new investment is the next step in a multi-year relationship between Robigo and Leaps, Bayer’s venture arm.
“They are not just developing a single product but rather building an engine that can rapidly address diverse soil-borne pathogens across broadacre crops,” Dr. Juergen Eckhardt, EVP and head of Leaps by Bayer, noted in a statement.
Robigo raised its seed round at the end of 2022, closing in early 2023. Wallace acknowledged the difficulty of the current climate but said the company’s ability to put field data on the table made the difference.
The Series A will also fund continued registration work. Robigo has already initiated the regulatory process for its soybean seed treatment product, another milestone Wallace flagged as significant for an engineered-organism product category that is still defining its regulatory path.

Apollo Funds Complete €3 Billion Capital Solution for Bayer
September 16, 2026 3:00am EDT 
Download as PDF
KKR joins Apollo as a minority participant
NEW YORK and LEVERKUSEN, Germany, Sept. 16, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Apollo (NYSE: APO) today announced that Apollo-managed funds and affiliates (“Apollo”) have successfully closed a €3 billion capital solution for Bayer, previously announced on July 10. KKR has joined Apollo as a significant minority participant in the investment.
Under the transaction, Apollo, together with KKR, have invested equity capital into a newly established entity holding Bayer's long-acting reversible contraceptives (LARC) business. Bayer retains a majority stake in the entity and continues to exercise full operational control over the business; there are no changes to the LARC strategy as a result of the investment.
Apollo Partner Jamshid Ehsani said, “We are proud to serve as a capital partner to Bayer, originating and leading a multi-billion-euro capital solution tailored to their needs. Bayer, a global life sciences leader and iconic German company, represents the types of large, blue-chip companies we serve through our High Grade Capital Solutions business.”
Ehsani added, “Apollo has committed to deploying more than $100 billion in Germany over the coming decade, and Bayer exemplifies the kind of strategic, long-term partnership we seek to build with the country's most important companies.”
Centerview Partners served as financial advisor to the Apollo Funds. Latham & Watkins LLP, Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison LLP, and NautaDutilh N.V. are legal counsel to the Apollo Funds.
About Apollo 
Apollo is a high-growth, global alternative asset manager. In our asset management business, we seek to provide our clients excess return at every point along the risk-reward spectrum from investment grade credit to private equity. For more than three decades, our investing expertise across our fully integrated platform has served the financial return needs of our clients and provided businesses with innovative capital solutions for growth. Through Athene, our retirement services business, we specialize in helping clients achieve financial security by providing a suite of retirement savings products and acting as a solutions provider to institutions. Our patient, creative and knowledgeable approach to investing aligns our clients, businesses we invest in, our employees and the communities we impact, to expand opportunity and achieve positive outcomes. As of June 30, 2026, Apollo had approximately $1.05 trillion of assets under management. To learn more, please visit www.apollo.com.
About Bayer 
Bayer is a global enterprise with core competencies in the life science fields of health care and nutrition. In line with its mission, “Health for all, Hunger for none,” the company’s products and services are designed to help people and the planet thrive by supporting efforts to master the major challenges presented by a growing and aging global population. Bayer is committed to driving sustainable development and generating a positive impact with its businesses. At the same time, the Group aims to increase its earning power and create value through innovation and growth. The Bayer brand stands for trust, reliability and quality throughout the world. In fiscal 2025, the Group employed around 88,000 people and had sales of 45.6 billion euros. R&D expenses amounted to 5.8 billion euros. For more information, go to www.bayer.com.
About KKR 
KKR is a leading global investment firm that offers alternative asset management as well as capital markets and insurance solutions. KKR aims to generate attractive investment returns by following a patient and disciplined investment approach, employing world-class people, and supporting growth in its portfolio companies and communities. KKR sponsors investment funds that invest in private equity, credit and real assets and has strategic partners that manage hedge funds. KKR’s insurance subsidiaries offer retirement, life and reinsurance products under the management of Global Atlantic Financial Group. References to KKR’s investments may include the activities of its sponsored funds and insurance subsidiaries. For additional information about KKR & Co. Inc. Mayo Clinic teams with Thermo Fisher to form biomedical data group Precure
By
Joseph Keenan 
Sep 15, 2026 11:46am 
Mayo Clinic 
Thermo Fisher Scientific 
partnership 
Big Data 
The Mayo Clinic and Thermo Fisher Scientific formed a group to reap data that could lead to the development of new treatments, devices and diagnostics. ()
The Mayo Clinic has partnered with Thermo Fisher Scientific to launch a new group focused on reaping large-scale data that could lead to the understanding and development of new treatments, devices and diagnostics.
The newly formed Precure LLC is tasked with creating one of the largest biomedical datasets using human multi-omics data generation that integrates proteomic, genomic and longitudinal clinical data to help identify early biological signals of disease, the clinic said in a release.
The goal is to better understand and identify early biological signals that develop before a disease is clinically diagnosed. By connecting molecular and clinical data early on, researchers could get a head start that could lead to faster drug development and earlier diagnosis across a wide range of diseases, including cancer, cardiometabolic disease, neurological disorders and immune-mediated disease. 
Related
Thermo Fisher Scientific teams up with Nvidia, TetraScience for next-gen AI workflow projects 
“Precure has the potential to create a step change in how we generate and apply multi-omics data to improve human health,” Marc Casper, Thermo Fisher Scientific’s chair and CEO, said in a statement. 
“By combining Thermo Fisher's leadership in scientific technology with Mayo Clinic's leadership in clinical care, research and innovation, we can create new opportunities at unprecedented scale to detect disease earlier, accelerate drug development and enable more precise therapies.”
The newly formed group is designed to complement Mayo Clinic’s Precure Research, which is part of an effort to gain insight into biological changes that happen as people move from health toward disease.
Precure Research looks to identify early disease signals while Precure LLC would provide the scale and infrastructure for collecting molecular data that could lead to new diagnostics, therapies and other solutions.
Mayo Clinic said any financial returns it earned from the endeavor would be used to further its mission of patient care, research and education.

EDGE, Safran to Build Sovereign Missile Propulsion Systems in Brazil 
Rojoef Manuel September 15, 2026 1 minute read

UAE’s state-owned company EDGE Group has signed an agreement with France’s Safran Electronics & Defense to establish solid rocket motor development and production capabilities in Brazil.
The initiative focuses on building local propulsion and guidance technology at EDGE’s Brazilian offshoot SIATT, which operates in the southeast city of São José dos Campos.
The cooperation will encompass other products such as guided weapons, loitering munitions, coastal defense, and core subsystems, including inertial navigation, GNSS receivers, actuators, optronic sights, and seekers.
According to the businesses, the move is expected to reduce external supply chain reliance for Brasília’s broader defense programs, including its armed forces’ Blue Amazon Management System or SisGAAz maritime surveillance network initiative.
It will also strengthen Safran’s long-standing position as an industrial partner for Brazil in almost five decades.
“This agreement extends our global partnership network to Brazil, bringing Safran Electronics & Defense together with SIATT to build solid rocket motor capabilities on Brazilian soil,” said Hamad Al Marar , CEO and managing director at EDGE Group.
He added that the deal reflects EDGE’s commitment to “strengthening sovereign defence capability for our partners.”
Alexandre Ziegler , head of the Defense Business Unit at Safran Electronics & Defense, echoed that sentiment, saying that the arrangement pushes forward the consortium’s “complementary expertise” to advance defense solutions across the region.
Other Projects
The deal follows a series of milestones for EDGE in Brazil as it grows its footprint in South America.
The Emirati group recently integrated an engineering segment through the acquisition of local firm AKAER and inaugurated a new SIATT production headquarters in the country.
The enterprise also established a cyber defense center with the Brazilian Army and expanded maritime project agreements with the Brazilian Navy .

From electronics to agriculture: How 3M film technology is helping manage light in new ways
Sep 15, 2026
Print current page. 
Send current page by email. 
Share current page on facebook. 
Share on Linkedin. 
Share current page on X 
For decades, 3M has applied optical film technology to help manage light in precise and useful ways, including in electronic devices and displays where light control can support brightness, clarity and energy efficiency. Now, that same expertise is being adapted for a new challenge: filtering sunlight to help support agriculture while also helping generate renewable energy.
Through an ongoing partnership with Voltiris , 3M is helping advance spectral-filtering solar technology designed to selectively manage sunlight above crops. The approach aims to let plants receive the light they need for growth while redirecting other portions of the light spectrum they don’t to help generate electricity.
Building on work in greenhouse agriculture, the companies recently launched an outdoor pilot in the Canary Islands to test how Voltiris’ Voltimax spectral-filtering module performs in open-field conditions.
For 3M, the pilot is part of a bigger story: applying an existing technology platform in a new way through external collaboration.
Your browser does not support the video tag. 
A new use for a core 3M technology platform 
3M’s role in the Voltiris partnership is rooted in its long-standing expertise in optical films, materials science and light management.
Optical films are designed to control how light is transmitted, reflected or redirected. In this pilot application, that expertise helps support a system that filters sunlight above crops, balancing two goals that are often in tension: protecting plants from excess heat while capturing solar energy.
That capability is what makes the collaboration different from a traditional solar installation. Rather than simply placing panels near agricultural land, the technology is designed to work with the growing environment by managing the spectrum of light reaching the crops.
For growers, that could create a valuable combination: improved growing conditions and renewable energy generation from the same footprint.
Why the Canary Islands pilot matters now 
The new pilot is in Gran Canaria, Spain, over a banana farm operated by Grupo FSM, the largest banana producer and exporter in Europe.
Bananas are central to the region’s agricultural economy, but they are grown in a challenging environment with high solar irradiance and significant heat stress. A large share of irrigation relies on desalinated water, where production requires substantial amounts of energy. In the Canary Islands, the electricity used for desalination represents a significant share of the total cost of banana production.
That makes the region a strong test case for a solution designed to address multiple pressures at once.
The pilot will explore whether spectral-filtering solar technology can help reduce heat stress for crops while also generating electricity that is expected to partially supply a desalination plant used for irrigation.
From greenhouse innovation to open-field agriculture 
3M and Voltiris have been working together for several years to help move the technology from concept toward broader application.
The solution has already been deployed at industrial scale in greenhouses across Europe. The Canary Islands pilot represents the next step: testing how the technology performs outdoors, where conditions are less controlled and durability, system performance and environmental exposure become even more important.
That shift from greenhouse to open-field agriculture is a meaningful expansion of the opportunity.
It also reflects how 3M works with partners to advance innovation: combining 3M’s science, technology platforms and application expertise with external companies developing new market solutions.
“In high-tech greenhouses across Northern Europe, where every percentage point of light matters, our technology has demonstrated that crops can thrive beneath Voltiris modules. Results show plant temperatures reduced by around 4°C and irrigation needs lowered by approximately 20%,” said Jonas Roch, chief technology officer and co-founder of Voltiris. “As heatwaves become more frequent and intense, our agrivoltaic solution helps make agriculture more resilient. We are now bringing the same principle outdoors, with the potential to deliver similar - or even greater - benefits while also protecting crops from wind, frost, hail, and heavy rain.”
Innovation through partnership 
“The collaboration with Voltiris demonstrates the value of combining 3M’s materials science expertise with external innovation to help accelerate emerging technologies,” said Mark Copman, senior vice president of 3M Ventures. “Together, we are advancing solutions that have the potential to support both agriculture and energy, while reflecting 3M’s ongoing commitment to applying science to complex global challenges.”
The partnership is an example of the way 3M works with innovators across industries: taking core technology platforms and applying them in new ways to help solve customer and market challenges.
In this case, 3M’s optical film expertise is helping enable a new approach to agricultural solar technology - one that could support crop environments, help generate renewable power and address resource pressures in regions where sunlight is abundant but conditions are increasingly demanding.
FAQ 
What is 3M’s partnership with Voltiris? 
3M is working with Voltiris to help advance spectral-filtering solar technology for agriculture. The collaboration combines Voltiris’ solar module innovation with 3M’s materials science and optical film expertise to explore new ways of managing sunlight above crops.
What role does 3M technology play? 
3M contributes expertise in optical films and light management. In this application, that technology helps support a system designed to filter sunlight so crops can receive the light they need while other portions of the spectrum are redirected to generate electricity.
What is new about the Canary Islands pilot? 
The Canary Islands pilot is the first outdoor deployment of Voltiris’ Voltimax spectral-filtering solar module for open-field agriculture. It provides a real-world test in a region where banana growers face high solar exposure, crop heat stress and energy-intensive irrigation needs.
How does this reflect 3M innovation? 
The partnership shows how 3M can apply a core technology platform in a new way through collaboration. By adapting optical film expertise for agriculture and renewable energy, 3M is helping advance a solution designed to address multiple challenges at once: crop conditions, energy generation and resource efficiency.

discovery_snippet: HS Hyosung, Umicore to Invest 1.2 Trillion Won in Ulsan Silicon Anode Plant    THE ELEC, Korea Electronics Industry Media
content_text:
HS Hyosung Energy Solution Korea a joint venture between HS Hyosung Group and Belgian materials company Umicore, will invest 1.2 trillion won to build a silicon anode materials production base in Ulsan.
​HS Hyosung Energy Solution Korea said Sept. 14 that it signed a memorandum of understanding with Ulsan Metropolitan City to build a silicon anode materials production plant. The company plans to invest a total of 1.2 trillion won through 2030 at the Ulsan-Mipo National Industrial Complex.
​The investment will be carried out in three phases. In the first phase, the company will invest 300 billion won to build MPK-1, a silicon anode materials plant with an annual capacity of 5,000 tons, by the first quarter of 2028. Further investment will follow to establish a mass-production system.
​Silicon anode materials have a higher energy density than conventional graphite-based anode materials, allowing electric vehicles to travel farther and charge faster.
​HS Hyosung Energy Solution Korea was established by HS Hyosung Group and Umicore for the silicon anode materials business, with an 80% to 20% ownership split. The venture is the first new business pursued by HS Hyosung Group since its separation from the wider Hyosung Group.
​Lee Ki-soo, chief executive officer of HS Hyosung Energy Solution Korea, said, "As we have selected Ulsan as our first investment site, we will grow together with the region by building an advanced production base and creating jobs."

title: Fortaegis Raises $50 Million to Secure AI Infrastructure at The Silicon Level - AI Insider

content_text:
Fortaegis Raises $50 Million to Secure AI Infrastructure at The Silicon Level
By Matt Swayne · 14 September 2026 · 5 min read 
Fortaegis raised $50 million to commercialize chip-based security technology for AI infrastructure, autonomous systems and connected machines. 
Insider Brief 
Fortaegis raised $50 million to commercialize chip-based security technology for AI infrastructure, autonomous systems and connected machines. 
Its architecture uses the unique physical properties of silicon chips to generate changing encryption keys and verify identities across networks. 
The funding will support commercial production, FPGA deployments and development of application-specific chips in the U.S., Europe and Asia.
Dutch startup Fortaegis has raised $50 million to commercialize a security architecture that uses the physical properties of silicon chips to protect AI infrastructure, autonomous systems and connected machines.
The oversubscribed Series A was led by Singapore-based Serendipity Capital , according to the company. Participants included TEL Venture Capital , the corporate venture arm of chip-equipment maker Tokyo Electron, as well as TNO , Prodrive Technologies , NP-Hard Ventures , NovaCapital , Access Ventures and Coalition Capital .
Fortaegis plans to use the funding to move from technology testing into commercial production and deployment. The company expects to begin commercial manufacturing in 2027, the Financial Times reported.
Founded in October 2023, Fortaegis says it is working with more than 25 companies and governments across AI infrastructure, defense, telecommunications, semiconductor manufacturing and other critical industries. Its government work includes organizations in the U.S., U.K., Japan, Singapore, Germany, France and the Netherlands, according to the FT.
“The security and prosperity of the West and its allies increasingly depend on who controls the foundations of compute. AI and quantum are making that question more urgent. Fortaegis was founded on the conviction that security cannot remain something we add on top of digital systems — it must become part of the foundations of compute itself. This investment allows us to accelerate that mission globally,” founder and CEO Boudewijn Wijnands said in the announcement.
Ilyas Khan, chair and founding shareholder of Fortaegis, said the architecture could become a widely used security layer as AI and quantum technologies develop.
“AI and quantum computing are not incremental shifts; they are changing the architecture of computing itself. Having founded and then built Quantinuum, I have seen how technologies that begin at the frontier can become foundational infrastructure. Fortaegis has the technology and ambition to do the same forSecure Compute — making security intrinsic to computing from silicon upward — and will become one of the hottest companies around as it becomes integral and essential for the rollout of compute in the next decades. Remember the name!” said Khan, who is also founder of the quantum computing company Quantinuum.
Security for Autonomous AI
Fortaegis is positioning its technology as a way to establish trust among AI systems, devices and data-center equipment without relying entirely on software.
That issue could become more important as companies deploy autonomous AI agents that can make decisions, access information and interact with other systems with limited human supervision. Large networks of agents and devices must be able to verify one another’s identities and determine whether instructions and data are authentic.
The Fortaegis Silicon Platform spans hardware, firmware, cryptography and software. It uses tiny physical variations created during semiconductor manufacturing to give each chip a unique digital fingerprint.
Fortaegis extracts information from that fingerprint to generate and frequently change encryption keys. The company says the keys are not permanently stored on devices, reducing the opportunity for attackers to locate and steal them.
The architecture is designed to extend identity checks, security policies and system management across potentially millions of devices and AI agents. Fortaegis says it can be deployed through data-center server racks, ruggedized systems for military, industrial and other demanding environments, compact edge devices or technology embedded directly into chips.
“Computing infrastructure is the central arena of geopolitical and economic competition today. As AI advances and quantum computing takes off, security and control of computing foundations are essential. Fortaegis is addressing that challenge at the architectural level,” said Chris Miller, a Fortaegis U.S. board member and author of “Chip War.”
AI and Quantum Risks Converge
The growth of AI is increasing the amount of sensitive information moving among data centers, processors, sensors and autonomous devices. At the same time, future quantum computers could undermine widely used encryption methods that protect much of that information.
Fortaegis describes its architecture as naturally quantum-safe because its keys are derived from the physical properties of silicon rather than generated solely through mathematical processes. Wijnands told the FT that a quantum computer would not have a mathematical model it could use to reconstruct those keys.
The quantum-safe claim will require broader independent analysis. The FT reported that national laboratories in several countries have validated the technology, but the article did not identify all the laboratories or provide detailed test results and threat models.
TNO, the Netherlands Organisation for Applied Scientific Research, has tested the technology. Marc Zegveld, head of the TNO group that conducted the assessment, told the FT that researchers used aggressive hacking methods but could not penetrate the integrated architecture.
Moving Toward Commercial Production
Fortaegis said customer-funded development programs are progressing from technical validation into production qualification and commercial deployment. The company has filed 17 patents and has another 14 in development.
The new funding will support production of Fortaegis products built with field-programmable gate arrays, or FPGAs, across the U.S., Europe, Singapore and Japan. FPGAs are chips that can be configured for particular tasks after manufacturing.
The company will also advance its development of application-specific integrated circuits, or ASICs. These are chips manufactured to perform defined functions and could allow Fortaegis to embed its security architecture more directly into commercial products.
“Secure Compute will become increasingly important across many industries. Fortaegis has developed a strong foundational technology, and we are committed to supporting its transition to scalable production and deployment,” said Peter Janssen, founder and chief technology officer of Prodrive Technologies.
Fortaegis says internal and customer testing has demonstrated connection performance more than 200 times faster than conventional approaches. The company and the FT did not provide detailed benchmarks identifying the protocols, hardware or network conditions used in that comparison.
The startup is also working with ASML and Eindhoven University of Technology on a security framework for autonomous AI systems. It is in talks with U.S. hyperscale cloud providers and AI laboratories, according to the FT.
“The most consequential deep-tech companies do more than improve an existing category — they create a new layer of infrastructure. We invested in Fortaegis because it is building exactly that: an architecture spanning silicon, hardware and software for a security challenge that becomes more important as AI, autonomy and quantum computing scale. We believe Secure Compute will own the foundational layer across both commercial and national-security infrastructure,” Serendipity Capital founder and CEO Rob Jesudason said.
